name: Stem Separation and Restoration
title: Stem Separation and Restoration
answer: Stem separation and restoration covers splitting a mixed recording into isolated sources such as vocals, drums, bass, and other instruments, and repairing degraded audio by reducing noise, clicks, clipping, and reverberation. It is used in remixing, mastering, archival work, film and game audio, and music education. The field sits within music composition and audio engineering, where the goal is often to recover usable material from recordings that were never tracked separately or have deteriorated. Modern tools make this practical on ordinary computers, but the quality depends heavily on the source material and the model used.

It is used in remixing, mastering, archival work, film and game audio, and music education. The field sits within music composition and audio engineering, where the goal is often to recover usable material from recordings that were never tracked separately or have deteriorated. Modern tools make this practical on ordinary computers, but the quality depends heavily on the source material and the model used.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Stem separation models typically run on consumer GPUs or cloud instances, with many services offering CPU fallback for shorter clips. Training requires large paired datasets of isolated stems and full mixes, which are expensive to create and often drawn from commercially released multitracks. Inference for a three-minute song can take seconds to a few minutes depending on model size and hardware. Restoration models often run as real-time or offline plugins inside digital audio workstations, using smaller networks optimized for low latency.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Most modern stem separation uses deep neural networks, often convolutional or transformer architectures, trained to estimate a mask or a direct waveform for each target source from a spectrogram or raw audio. Restoration typically combines learned models with classical signal processing, such as spectral subtraction for noise or phase reconstruction for clipped peaks. Engineers often iterate between automatic separation and manual cleanup, using the stems as a starting point rather than a finished product. Evaluation relies on objective metrics like signal-to-distortion ratio and subjective listening tests.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Separating stems from a copyrighted recording can raise questions about derivative works, licensing, and moral rights, especially when the output is republished or used in new compositions. Restoration of archival material may involve ownership of the physical carrier, the underlying performance, and any restoration decisions made by an engineer. The site tracks 92 active intellectual property lawsuits, 18 of which involve AI music services, reflecting ongoing disputes over training data and output ownership. Provenance is a practical concern: a separated stem may contain artifacts or bleed from other sources, and a restored master may no longer represent the original release. Engineers typically document the model, version, and manual edits so that downstream users can assess what was changed.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Separation quality is improving for dense mixes and live recordings, with models becoming better at handling overlapping instruments and room acoustics. Restoration is moving toward more transparent repair of severe damage, including missing segments and heavily compressed audio, with less audible processing. On-device separation and restoration are becoming more common in consumer software and hardware, reducing the need for cloud uploads. The main open problems are preserving phase coherence, reducing artifacts on atypical sources, and establishing clearer norms for attribution and consent when stems are reused.
